html:
"Semites" is an old name for the peoples who spoke Semitic languages, across Mesopotamia, the Levant, Arabia and the Horn of Africa. On this map it covers Arabia and the desert fringes of the Fertile Crescent in 3000 and 2000 BCE. Today the term is used mainly for the languages, not for the peoples.

The family includes Akkadian, Amorite, Canaanite, Hebrew, Phoenician, Aramaic, Arabic and the languages of Ethiopia. Akkadian was the first to be written, in cuneiform, from around 2500 BCE. Sargon of Akkad built the Akkadian Empire, and Akkadian slowly replaced Sumerian in southern Mesopotamia.

Many Semitic speakers were herders on the steppe and desert edges, moving between pasture and the towns. Around 2000 BCE the Amorites spread from Syria into Mesopotamia and founded new dynasties, among them that of Babylon. In the west lived the people of Canaan. Later Semitic speakers gave the world the alphabet, through the Phoenicians, and three religions: Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
